solubility-equilibria-s1.title: Solubility products of four salts
solubility-equilibria-s1.text: A student looks up Ksp values (approximate, at 25 °C) for four slightly soluble salts.

solubility-equilibria-s2.title: A saturated solution of a salt
solubility-equilibria-s2.html:
Key: metal cation, M2+anion, X−

The diagram shows the dissolved ions above the undissolved solid in a saturated solution of a salt of M2+ and X− at 25 °C. Water molecules are not shown. Each ion drawn stands for 2.0 × 10−4 mol of ions per liter of solution.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: s² = K<sub>sp</sub>, so take the square root; do not divide by 2.
Value: AgCl gives one ion of each kind, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s², not 4s³.

why.correct: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻; [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s. K<sub>sp</sub> = s² = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in pure water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: Ag₂CrO₄ gives 2 Ag⁺ per formula unit. K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(s) = 4s³; take a cube root.
Value: you wrote 2s² × s. The silver concentration 2s must be squared as a whole: (2s)² = 4s².
Value: (2s)² = 4s², so K<sub>sp</sub> = 4s³. Divide by 4 before the cube root.

why.correct: Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2 Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻; [Ag⁺] = 2s, [CrO₄²⁻] = s. K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², so s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³ and s = 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M.

items.q: Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> has a smaller K<sub>sp</sub> than AgCl. Which salt has the greater molar solubility in water?
options: Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>
AgCl
They are equally soluble, because both are silver salts.
It is undecided without the masses of the salts.

why.correct: Ranking by K<sub>sp</sub> works only for salts with the same ion ratio. Otherwise, calculate the molar solubility of each.
options: Right: 6.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M versus 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M. With different ion ratios, the K<sub>sp</sub> expressions have different forms, so K<sub>sp</sub> alone cannot be compared.
AgCl has the larger K<sub>sp</sub>, but the expressions differ (s² vs 4s³). Calculate s for each.
Sharing a cation does not make solubilities equal.
It can: solve each K<sub>sp</sub> expression for s.

items.q: Which pair of salts can be ranked by solubility just by comparing their K<sub>sp</sub> values?
options: AgCl and AgBr
AgCl and Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>
AgBr and CaF<sub>2</sub>
Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> and AgBr

why.correct: When two salts produce the same number and ratio of ions, their K<sub>sp</sub> expressions have the same form, so K<sub>sp</sub> ranks solubility directly.
options: Right: both are 1 : 1, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s² for each and a larger K<sub>sp</sub> means a larger s.
These have different ion ratios (1 : 1 and 2 : 1), so their expressions differ.
Different ion ratios: s² versus 4s³.
Different ion ratios: 4s³ versus s².

items.q: Calculate [F<sup>−</sup>] in a saturated solution of CaF<sub>2</sub> in water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: that is s, the molar solubility. Each CaF₂ gives two F⁻, so [F⁻] = 2s.
Value: CaF₂ gives 1 Ca²⁺ and 2 F⁻, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³.

items.q: What is the formula of the salt?
options: MX<sub>2</sub>
MX
M<sub>2</sub>X
M<sub>3</sub>X<sub>6</sub>

why.correct: Ions dissolve in the ratio of the formula: 3 M²⁺ to 6 X⁻ is 1 : 2, matching the charges: MX₂.
options: Right: the solution holds twice as many X⁻ as M²⁺, and the charges balance as 2+ and 2(1−).
MX would give equal numbers of each ion and leave a 1+ charge per formula unit.
This would give more cations than anions, the opposite of the diagram.
This is the count in the picture, not the simplest formula of the salt.

items.q: Use the diagram to calculate K<sub>sp</sub> for the salt.

mistakes.why: Value: [X⁻] is squared, because each MX₂ gives two X⁻ (coefficient 2).
Value: square [X⁻] rather than doubling it.
Value: you used particle counts. Convert each count to a concentration first (× 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M).

items.q: More solid MX<sub>2</sub> is added to the beaker and stirred at 25 °C. What happens to the number of dissolved ions?
options: It stays the same, because the solution is already saturated and the solid is not in K<sub>sp</sub>.
It increases, because more solid is available to dissolve.
It decreases, because the extra solid pulls ions out of solution.
It doubles, because the amount of solid doubled.

why.correct: A saturated solution is an equilibrium between solid and ions. Adding solid leaves Q = K<sub>sp</sub>, so the dissolved concentrations stay the same.
options: Right: the solid is left out of Q and K<sub>sp</sub>, so adding it does not change Q; the ion concentrations are already at their equilibrium values.
The dissolving rate and the precipitation rate are already equal. More solid does not change the ion concentrations at equilibrium.
Q still equals K<sub>sp</sub>; there is no net precipitation.
The amount of a pure solid does not enter K<sub>sp</sub>.

items.q: Which statement describes the particles in this beaker?
options: Ions leave the solid and ions return to it at equal rates.
No more ions dissolve, because the solution is full.
Ions dissolve, but ions no longer return to the solid.
The solid and the ions no longer interact.

why.correct: Like any equilibrium, a saturated solution is dynamic: dissolving and precipitation continue at equal rates.
options: Right: a saturated solution is a dynamic equilibrium between dissolving and precipitation.
Ions keep dissolving; just as many rejoin the solid each second.
Then the concentrations would keep rising and the solid would disappear.
Dissolved ions keep colliding with the solid surface and sticking to it.

items.q: A saturated solution of PbI<sub>2</sub> (molar mass 461.0 g/mol) contains 0.62 g of dissolved PbI<sub>2</sub> per liter at 25 °C. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: PbI₂ gives two I⁻, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³.
Value: square the whole [I⁻] = 2s: (2s)² = 4s².
Value: convert grams per liter to moles per liter first, using the molar mass.

items.q: The molar solubility of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> in water at 25 °C is 1.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: you did not square [OH⁻]. K<sub>sp</sub> = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² = s(2s)².
Value: [OH⁻] is 2s, not s. Each Mg(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻.
Value: Mg(OH)₂ is not a 1 : 1 salt. Use [OH⁻] = 2s and square it.

items.q: Which is the K<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(s) ⇌ 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>(aq)?
options: [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>
[Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> / [Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]
3[Ca<sup>2+</sup>] × 2[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]
[Ca<sup>2+</sup>][PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]

why.correct: K<sub>sp</sub> is the product of the ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient; the solid is left out.
options: Right: the solid is left out, and each ion is raised to its coefficient.
The solid is a pure solid, so it does not appear in K<sub>sp</sub>.
Coefficients are exponents, not multipliers.
Each concentration must be raised to its coefficient.

items.q: Equal volumes of 2.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M AgNO<sub>3</sub> and 2.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M NaCl are mixed. K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl is 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. Does AgCl precipitate?
options: Yes: Q = 1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> > K<sub>sp</sub>.
No: Q = 1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> < K<sub>sp</sub>.
Yes: Q = 4.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> > K<sub>sp</sub>.
No: both solutions are too dilute to form a solid.

why.correct: Compare the ion product Q with K<sub>sp</sub>. After mixing, [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M; Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > K<sub>sp</sub>, so solid AgCl forms until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
options: Right: mixing equal volumes halves each concentration to 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M, and Q = (1.0 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Compare powers of ten: 10⁻⁸ is larger than 10⁻¹⁰.
The conclusion is right but Q is wrong: mixing equal volumes halves each concentration before you multiply.
Dilution matters only through Q; here Q is still far above K<sub>sp</sub>.

items.q: Put the steps for finding molar solubility from K<sub>sp</sub> in order.
options: Write the dissolving equation, with the ions in the ratio of the formula.
Let s be the molar solubility and write each ion concentration as s times its coefficient.
Write K<sub>sp</sub> with each ion concentration raised to its coefficient, e.g. s(2s)<sup>2</sup> = 4s<sup>3</sup>.
Solve for s and report it in mol/L.

why.correct: Equation, ion concentrations in terms of s, K<sub>sp</sub> expression with exponents, solve.

items.q: The dissolving of a salt in water is endothermic. A saturated solution with excess solid is warmed. What happens?
options: More solid dissolves, because K<sub>sp</sub> increases.
Solid precipitates, because K<sub>sp</sub> increases.
Nothing, because K<sub>sp</sub> is a constant.
More solid dissolves, because Q increases.

why.correct: K<sub>sp</sub> is an equilibrium constant, so it changes with temperature. For endothermic dissolving, heating increases K<sub>sp</sub> and the solubility.
options: Right: for an endothermic dissolving process, K<sub>sp</sub> rises with temperature, so Q < K<sub>sp</sub> and more solid dissolves.
A larger K<sub>sp</sub> means more ions can be in solution, so solid dissolves rather than precipitates.
K<sub>sp</sub> is constant only at a fixed temperature.
Warming does not change the ion concentrations at once, so Q does not change. K<sub>sp</sub> does.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> is 5.0 × 10<sup>−6</sup> at 25 °C. Calculate [OH<sup>−</sup>] in a saturated solution.

mistakes.why: Value: that is s, the molar solubility. Each Ca(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 2s.
Value: Ca(OH)₂ gives three ions, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³; use a cube root.
Value: (2s)² = 4s², so K<sub>sp</sub> = 4s³, not 2s³.

items.q: The molar solubility of Ag<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> in water is 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M at 25 °C. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: [Ag⁺] = 3s must be cubed as a whole: (3s)³ = 27s³.
Value: [Ag⁺] is 3s, not s. K<sub>sp</sub> = (3s)³(s) = 27s⁴.
Value: raise [Ag⁺] = 3s to the power 3, its coefficient: K<sub>sp</sub> = (3s)³(s).

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of BaSO<sub>4</sub> (molar mass 233.39 g/mol) is 1.1 × 10<sup>−10</sup> at 25 °C. Calculate the mass of BaSO<sub>4</sub> that dissolves in 1.00 L of water.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the molar solubility in mol/L. Multiply by 1.00 L and by the molar mass to get grams.
Value: take the square root of K<sub>sp</sub> first; K<sub>sp</sub> = s² for a 1 : 1 salt.

items.q: A saturated solution of AgCl is in contact with excess solid at 25 °C. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [Cl<sup>−</sup>] if no other source of either ion is present.
Adding more water and stirring dissolves more solid, but [Ag<sup>+</sup>] ends up the same.
K<sub>sp</sub> is larger when more solid is present.
No AgCl dissolves once the solution is saturated.

why.correct: In a saturated solution the ion concentrations are fixed by K<sub>sp</sub> at a given temperature. More water dissolves more solid in total, but the concentrations come back to the same values.
options: Right: each AgCl that dissolves gives one of each ion.
Right: once saturated again, the concentrations return to the values set by K<sub>sp</sub>.
The solid is not in K<sub>sp</sub>; its amount does not matter.
Dissolving continues, balanced by precipitation at the same rate.
